author: ohtadmin
title: Council considering rec committee
text:
An appointed public body to collaborate with the department of parks and recreation is being considered by the town council.
The department’s director, Ray DeFalco, briefed the councilors at their July 20 meeting about other cities and towns with these committees. He presented a spreadsheet of the 38 municipalities with notes on their rec commissions, including their authority and staffing structure. Twenty-five have rec boards. Block Island’s, for example, “is charged with advising the town council and making recommendations regarding matters that support the mission of the recreation department to provide leisure and active recreation programming that will promote the general health, welfare and personal development of the community.”
“Most serve in an advisory capacity,” DeFalco said. “The commissions that are reported to be most helpful are those that work closely with the parks and recreation director and staff.”
DeFalco said smaller commissions, with five members, “also tend to operate more efficiently … with fewer reported meeting cancellations and more productive discussions.”
“If you have knowledgeable people on them and they’re directed with a proper charge, that could be beneficial to the rec department,” Councilwoman Mary Meagher said.
Erik Brine, the council’s vice president, asked whether commissions in other cities and towns collaborate with ex officio members and liaisons.
“Each community is different,” DeFalco replied. “You have to think about who has a stake in the parks and recreation in that town. That’s why some of them have school committee members, some of them don’t. Some of them have a town council liaison, some of them don’t. It also depends on the size of the community.”
“We’re interested,” said the council’s president, Nancy Beye. “We’re curious.”
Town Administrator Ed Mello, after hearing the council’s support for exploring the proposal, recommended giving DeFalco’s staff “a little bit of time to put some thought into it and start to draft a charge.”
Mello also suggested consolidating some committees. For example, the bike committee and the Eldred Field board could be merged with the proposed rec commission.
The reason to consolidate, Mello said, is some committees “ask a lot of the staff at times.” Fewer committees means fewer requests for assistance. Also, Mello added, a singular commission could prioritize proposals rather than each separate board fighting for their own improvements.
“There’s an opportunity to be more in lockstep,” Mello said.
“Sort of like your dream team,” Brine added.
The 13 municipalities without rec commissions are Jamestown, Exeter, West Greenwich, East Greenwich, Middletown, Smithfield, Central Falls, Newport, Johnston, Coventry, Woonsocket, Warwick and Providence. West Greenwich is the only city or town in Rhode Island without a municipal department for parks and recreation.
